question: Why does HeyGen call Avatar 6 84.4% indistinguishable from real video when raters picked it as the real one only 42.2% of the time?

rungs.question: Why does a 42.2% pick rate become an 84.4% headline?
rungs.answer: HeyGen defines its indistinguishability rate as twice the share of side-by-side choices that picked the Avatar 6 clip as real. A rater who could not tell the two apart would pick each half the time, so 50% scores as 100%. Raters picked the real recording 57.8% of the time and the avatar 42.2%, which doubles to 84.4%.

evidence.quote: Side by side with the real recording, raters pick Avatar 6 as the real one 42.2% of the time. 50% would mean they cannot tell at all, so Avatar 6 is 84.4% of the way there.
We report this as the indistinguishability rate, twice the share of choices that pick the Avatar 6
external raters selected Avatar 6 as the real recording in 42.2% of 270 side-by-side answers, and the score doubles that selection rate because 50% would represent chance

HeyGen divides 42.2 by 50 and doubles the result to get 84.4%, which is a legitimate way to express "how far across the gap did we get" and a misleading way to express "how often does this fool someone."

counter.text: The arithmetic is not disputed by any source read; the dispute is over the unit. orcarouter.ai calls 84.4% "a real result expressed in a flattering unit". HeyGen's technical report says a further 11.2% of the 304 side-by-side answers were "can't tell" and were left out of the 270 answers the 42.2% is counted on; the research page's headline does not mention them.

rungs.question: Why could the avatar clips come that close to the real ones in the test?
rungs.answer: The test gave Avatar 6 its strongest input. Each HeyGen employee's real recording was split in two: the model saw the first part as a reference and regenerated the second part, saying the same sentence over the same real audio, and raters compared that with the held-out real part.

evidence.quote: Each person’s footage is split; Avatar 6 sees only the reference part and generates the
Real vs Avatar 6, same sentence over the same audio.
raters were shown a real recording and an Avatar 6 clip of the same person saying the same sentence over the same audio, and picked Avatar 6 as the real one 42.2% of the time

counter.text: Shown alone rather than side by side, Avatar 6 clips with the person's own voice were judged real in 65.1% of answers against 78.9% for real recordings, and 56.5% with a HeyGen Voice clone. The side-by-side part covers 76 people and 20 external raters, on HeyGen employees' footage; orcarouter.ai says "All of these are HeyGen's own studies". The one outside test both news sources cite, New Measure's Avatar Arena, ranked Avatar 6 first on preference, not on passing as real, with clips of 35 seconds or less in 97% of comparisons.

rungs.question: Why does the footage-driven test not describe what the photo route does?
rungs.answer: HeyGen runs two routes with different rules. A footage avatar cannot render until the person records an on-camera consent statement with a one-time code. A photo reference, open to all workspaces, needs no agreement, only the person's permission; video reference is for enterprise customers. The 84.4% figure was measured on the footage route.

evidence.quote: Before an avatar created from a person's footage can generate any video, the person must record a short on-camera consent statement that includes a one-time code generated for that session
Photo reference: a photo of the person, used with their permission. The model generates the motion.All workspacesNo agreement neededNot required
Photo references are available to all API workspaces with the person’s permission, whereas realistic video references are enterprise-only.

counter.text: The developer docs, repeated by unite.ai, say some video-reference contracts also run without a consent step: "Some contracts run without a consent step, reviewed case by case." A realistic reference video from a workspace without access returns an error. orcarouter.ai calls the footage consent design "stricter than most avatar vendors bother with". None of the sources reports a Turing test on the photo-only route.

rungs.question: Why does HeyGen check consent on recorded footage but rely on stated permission for a single photo?
rungs.answer: Nothing read answers it. The sources state the two rules side by side but give no reason for the difference.

counter.text: none found in the HeyGen research page, the technical report, the developer docs, unite.ai, orcarouter.ai and the csuite.so roundup

landing.shows: The 84.4% is HeyGen's own rescaling of a 42.2% pick rate, measured by HeyGen on its employees' footage, with the avatar regenerating half of a real recording over the real audio and with the 11.2% of "can't tell" answers left out. That footage route sits behind a one-time-code consent check; the photo route, open to every workspace, needs no agreement and has no Turing number in the sources.
landing.open_question: If the headline realism was measured on the route that checks consent, how real does the route that only asks for permission look?
